messages.subject: [S] : Summary - Data extraction using unpaste
messages.body_plain:
I received one response from Don MacQueen to my question regarding the use
of unpaste to extract information from a column with a variable number of
delimited fields.  The solution arrived at is to pad the column so that all
rows have the same number of fields.  Then unpaste will allow extraction of
whatever element is desired without difficulty.

For the situation previously described the following steps suffice.

# count the number of fields in each row of the column
nfields <- count.fields.str(d.df$rate,sep="~")
# calculate the number of fields needed to pad
npad <- max(nfields)-nfields
# create a column of length(d.df$rate) with appropriate pad characters
padchars <- ifelse(npad==0,"",ifelse(npad==1,"~","~~"))
# pad column with appropriate number of field delimiters
d.df$rate <- paste(d.df$rate,padchars,sep="")
d.df$rateUnit <- paste(d.df$rateUnit,padchars,sep="")

# continue extraction of desired fields
d.df$okRate <- numeric(length(d.df$rate))
d.df$okRtun <- as.character(numeric(length(d.df$rate)))
for (i in min(d.df$posKey):max(d.df$posKey)){
  d.df$okRate[d.df$posKey==i]<-
as.numeric(unpaste(d.df$rate[d.df$posKey==i],sep="~")[[i]])
  d.df$okRtun[d.df$posKey==i]<-
as.character(unpaste(d.df$rateUnit[d.df$posKey==i],sep="~")[[i]])}

Feel free to comment as to better approches.  This approach does work, but
there is likely room for improvement.  And thanks to Don MacQueen for his
helpful suggestion.

Peter Scherer
Dow AgroSciences

Sent: Wednesday, February 09, 2000 12:10 PM
To: 's-news at wubios.wustl.edu'

Hello all,

I have a data extraction problem when using unpaste to crop out the field
information desired from the rate and rateUnit columns.  Below is a portion
of the data frame in question.

>
d.df[c(1,1000,2000,3000,4000),c("trtName","rate","rateUnit","nfName","posKey
")]

Where trtName, rate, rateUnit all have a variable number of fields delimited

nfName identifies the total number of fields for the given row 
and posKey identifies which field is desired for extraction.

I attempt to extract the pertinent rate and rateUnit information (denoted by
posKey) using the following construct

# extract associated rate and rate units using posKey
d.df$okRate <- numeric(length(d.df$rate))
d.df$okRtun <- as.character(numeric(length(d.df$rate)))
for (i in min(d.df$posKey):max(d.df$posKey)){

For those cases where posKey == nfName (note that nfName is not used in the
loop, but rather is the result of a separate calculation)  the results are
as desired.  However where posKey != nfName NA is the result with the
following warnings.

Warning messages:

unpaste(d.df$rate\
        [d.df$posKey == i], sep = "~")

        d.df$posKey == i], sep = "~")
4: 516 entries set to NA due to wrong number of fields in:

Note that there are 4783 cases where posKey==1 & nfName!=1 and 516 cases
where posKey==2 & nfName!=2

The error message comes from within unpaste, but if I manually extract the
last rate presented in the data frame above using
unpaste("~140~.25",sep="~")[[2]]  I get the desired result of 140.  I guess
I don't understand what is failing inside the loop and why.  Any insight,
suggestions, alternative approaches are most appreciated.

(I am using S-Plus 2000 on a 400mHz PC w/ 64 mg RAM.)

Thanks in advance,

messages.subject: [S] SUMMARY: leap() and repeated measures / lme()
messages.subject_clean: [S] SUMMARY: leap() and repeated measures / lme()
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Renaud Lancelot and Brian Ripley for their helpful responses!!!  

Here's my original question:
> 
> Is there anyone out there who has developed a routine for best-subsets
> regression when you're dealing with repeated measures data (e.g. when
> fitting lme() models)?  Or, does anyone happen to know how to 
> incorporate repeated measures into leap()?  I've searched StatLib and the 
> S-news archive and did not find anything.

And here are the responses:

1)This question is tricky. AFAIK, no such method is emplemented for mixed
model. The problem is that you cannot rely on likelihood ratio tests or
AIC / BIC to select the best submodel. Bates and Pinheiro have shown (in
their forthcoming book) that these tests often fail to reject the null
hypothesis. Therefore, it would not make sense to adapt functions such
as stepAIC() in MASS library or step() in "regular" S+2000. 

The method to select submodels is to perform t tests (or F tests when
you want to test several coefficients). These tests are provided in the
outputs of summary.lme and anova.lme (careful for the latter: you should
use the argument type = "marginal"). This is cumbersome when you have
many covariates (I precisely have this problem now !).

2)leaps (I assume you do mean leap*s*?) uses shortcuts in the
branch-and-bound search that only apply to least-squares fitting (and to
single variates rather than coded factors, say). Now `repeated measures' is
a description of data collection and not methods (see Diggle Liang and
Zeger's book for the gamut of possible approaches), but with mixed effect
models I see no alternative to a stepwise or brute-force search.  Does it
matter?  The examples where backwards selection is misleading are ones
where the collinearities in the data usually mean that the wrong variables
were used, anyway.  When one typed ones commands on punched cards, did one
run and wanted the right output on the line printer a best-subsets search
was convenient, but much less so now.

Thanks again!!!

-- Andy

messages.subject: [S] FW: covertion of long character vectors to dates
messages.subject_clean: [S] FW: covertion of long character vectors to dates
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Recently I posted a question how to conserve memory during conversion of
char strings to date. Don MacQueen suggested to use dateTime() class. This
is probably the best option, though I didn't test it because my dates were
encoded in a non-standard format. One of the disadvantages of this solution
is that dateTime class consumes twice as much memory as dates. This is
wasteful if you actually only need dates (without milliseconds), but one
shouldn't really care unless he works with huge volumes of data (as I do).

It turned out that the memory is consumed in the function julian() which
returns an object of class "named". Creation of those names is what kills
the call. This can be fixed by commenting out two lines in the source code
of julian().

In general it is best to avoid use of named objects for very large objects.
One of the functions that by default  creates a named object is unlist(),
see ?unlist for how to override the default.

Regards,
Vadim

Sent:   Thursday, February 10, 2000 3:30 PM

class. The call x _ dates(character.dates) dies after consuming more than

messages.subject: [S] Coefficients of the GLM
messages.body_plain:
Dear everyone,

I have great difficulties with the explanation of the coefficient
estimates of a GLM. To my knowledge, I understand that the coefficients
represent the means of the factor in a series. For example, I have a
factor "Year" that has a time of ten years. The GLM would produce ten
estimates: Intercept, year1, year2,...year9. The Intercept is the mean
of first year, "year1" is the mean of Year 2 relative to Year 1, and its
abosolute mean should be "Intercept+year1", and so on. Am I right?

However, the example S-Plus gave in its manual (S-Plus 4 Guide to
Statistics page 213) can not be explained this wage. A GLM with the data
of "solder.balance", the "Opening" factor has three levels, S, M, L. The
coefficients estimated are: Intercept=0.438,
Opening.L=-1.687,Opening.Q=0.462. The confusion here is what Opening.Q
means. If in order, Intercept shoudl refer to Opening at S level because
S is the first level in the data file, and then Opening.Q should mean
Opening at M level. If this is right, the mean of M level shoudl be the
highest and that of L level should be the lowest. But, the graph S-Plus
produced for the Openging effect was: S highest, M mediate, and L
lowest, which is consistent with the data file.

Your can easily test this with the command:
>paov2 <-glm(skips~.+(Opening+Solder+Mask+PadType)^2,
family=poison,data=solder.balance)
>summary(paov2)
>par(mfrow=c92,3)
>plot.gam(paov2,resid=T)

Can anybody expalin how the coefficient estimates and the graph should
be explained?

Thank you very much for your help.

messages.subject: Re: [S] Coefficients of the GLM
messages.body_plain:
Dear Yimin Ye,

S constructs contrasts (columns of the model matrix) for a factor according to 
the contrasts option. The default option is

> options()$contrasts
          factor      ordered 
 "contr.helmert" "contr.poly"

that is Helmert contrasts for an unordered factor, and orthogonal polynomials 
for an ordered factor. 

Opening is a three-category ordered factor (with therefore 2 df), and Opening.L 
and Opening.Q are, respectively, the linear and quadratic terms. Try 
contrasts(Opening) to see the contrast coding, here:

> contrasts(Opening)
          .L         .Q 
S -0.7071068  0.4082483
M  0.0000000 -0.8164966
L  0.7071068  0.4082483

By the way, Helmert contrasts do not simply treat the first category as the 
baseline -- to do this you need to use "treatment" contrasts, contr.treatment. 
You can change the global option, or assign a contrast attribute to the factor:

> contrasts(Opening)<-contr.helmert(3)
> contrasts(Opening)
  [,1] [,2] 
S   -1   -1
M    1   -1
L    0    2
>
> contrasts(Opening)<-contr.treatment(3)
> contrasts(Opening)
  2 3 
S 0 0
M 1 0
L 0 1

See ?contrasts and ?contr.treatment for more information.

plot.gam shows partial residuals and partial effect plots. These don't depend 
on the coding of contrasts.

I hope that this helps,

John

messages.subject: [S] Modeling models!
messages.body_plain:
Hello S-users,

in the last few months we have built several models P (i), i = 1, ..., n as
follows:

P (i) = f (i) c (i)

where f (i) was modeled as a Poisson variable, using glm with log link.
and c (i) was modeled as a Gamma variable, using glm with log link to insure
multiplicative models.

We are now interested to combine all those models as follows:

P (final) = P (1) + ... + P (n)

The factors used to model any of the f (i) and c (i) are available for all i, i
= 1, ..., n, hence we have parameter estimates for all levels of all available
factors; if a factor was not used in any one model the coefficients of all it's
levels are simply 0 for that one model.  Therefore to compute P (final) we need
n coefficients for each level of each factor plus coefficients for interaction
terms.

The challenge:

in the name of simplicity, and ease of implementation, we would like to
approximate the best estimate P (final) in order to obtain a single coefficient
per factor level.  Any hints?  Anything one should be particularly cautious
about?

Thanks very kindly for any insights,

On Wed, 16 Feb 2000, John Fox wrote:

> 
> Dear Yimin Ye,
> 
> S constructs contrasts (columns of the model matrix) for a factor according 
> to the contrasts option. The default option is
> 
> > options()$contrasts
>           factor      ordered 
>  "contr.helmert" "contr.poly"
> 
> that is Helmert contrasts for an unordered factor, and orthogonal polynomials 
> for an ordered factor. 
> 
> Opening is a three-category ordered factor (with therefore 2 df), and 
> Opening.L and Opening.Q are, respectively, the linear and quadratic terms. 
> Try contrasts(Opening) to see the contrast coding, here:
> 
> > contrasts(Opening)
>           .L         .Q 
> S -0.7071068  0.4082483
> M  0.0000000 -0.8164966
> L  0.7071068  0.4082483
> 
> 
> By the way, Helmert contrasts do not simply treat the first category as the 
> baseline -- to do this you need to use "treatment" contrasts, 
> contr.treatment. You can change the global option, or assign a contrast 
> attribute to the factor:
> 
> > contrasts(Opening)<-contr.helmert(3)
> > contrasts(Opening)
>   [,1] [,2] 
> S   -1   -1
> M    1   -1
> L    0    2
> >
> > contrasts(Opening)<-contr.treatment(3)
> > contrasts(Opening)
>   2 3 
> S 0 0
> M 1 0
> L 0 1
> 
> 
> See ?contrasts and ?contr.treatment for more information.
> 
> plot.gam shows partial residuals and partial effect plots. These don't depend 
> on the coding of contrasts.
> 
> I hope that this helps,
> 
> John
> 
> 
> 
> At 02:17 PM 2/16/2000 +0300, you wrote:
> >
> >Dear everyone,
> >
> >I have great difficulties with the explanation of the coefficient
> >estimates of a GLM. To my knowledge, I understand that the coefficients
> >represent the means of the factor in a series. For example, I have a
> >factor "Year" that has a time of ten years. The GLM would produce ten
> >estimates: Intercept, year1, year2,...year9. The Intercept is the mean
> >of first year, "year1" is the mean of Year 2 relative to Year 1, and its
> >abosolute mean should be "Intercept+year1", and so on. Am I right?
> >
> >However, the example S-Plus gave in its manual (S-Plus 4 Guide to
> >Statistics page 213) can not be explained this wage. A GLM with the data
> >of "solder.balance", the "Opening" factor has three levels, S, M, L. The
> >coefficients estimated are: Intercept=0.438,
> >Opening.L=-1.687,Opening.Q=0.462. The confusion here is what Opening.Q
> >means. If in order, Intercept shoudl refer to Opening at S level because
> >S is the first level in the data file, and then Opening.Q should mean
> >Opening at M level. If this is right, the mean of M level shoudl be the
> >highest and that of L level should be the lowest. But, the graph S-Plus
> >produced for the Openging effect was: S highest, M mediate, and L
> >lowest, which is consistent with the data file.

> >Your can easily test this with the command:

> >>par(mfrow=c92,3)

> >
> >Can anybody expalin how the coefficient estimates and the graph should
> >be explained?

messages.body_plain:
There are two places you can find state population data,
1. US Census Bureau @ www.census.gov. Census bureau updates their info every
ten years. The last info they have is 1990. They are collecting 2000 data
now;
2. State Department of Health. They have most current vital statistic data.

In Florida, DOH has its own website posting vital statistic data. Also, DOH
contracts with other agencies to publish statistic abstract book. I am not
sure did NC do the same thing or not. These information are open to publics,
you shouldn't have hard time to get it.

As of map, I assume you are talking about plotting your own data on
geographical maps. I didn't use S-Plus on this task, so couldn't give you
any suggestion. However, I did use Map.info and Archview mapping
geographical data. When purchasing these software, they come with geo. data
to county level. If you are going to handle data in smaller unit, such as
zip code, block, or tract, you need to purchase it. To match your data with
geo. coded data, your data need to be geocoded by address as well. This
requires another software.

Kwang-lee

messages.subject_clean: [S] Reading Many XL sheets into and S-plus dataframe: Summary
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to those who responded to my inquiry. 

I ultimately solved the problem by having my local Visual Basic guru (Chris
Gent) create 
a program that outputs  the tab (worksheet) name and the data in the first 8
rows and 12 columns
as a (9 n x 12)  ASCII file (n = number of worksheets). I was then able to
import and reshape the data for analysis.
This has inspired me to try to learn more about Visual Basic.

Here are a few other ideas: 

*****************************************************************
Julie Green  (julie at statsci.com) came up with the following function that
can read many pages if you are
willing to hand enter the tab (worksheet) names.

pagenum= number of pages to read
vec.names= names of workbook pages

demo.tmp <- function(pagnum, vec.names) {
        for (i in 1:pagnum) {
        import.data(FileName = "C:\\testspl.xls",
        FileType = "Excel",
        ColNames = "",
        Format = "",
        TargetStartCol = "1",
        DataFrame = vec.names[i],
        NameRow = "0",
        StartCol = "1",
        EndCol = "12",
        StartRow = "1",
        EndRow = "8",
        Delimiters = ", \\t",
        SeparateDelimiters = F,
        PageNumber = paste(i),
        RowNameCol = "0",
        StringsAsFactors = "Auto",
        VLabelAsNumber = F,
        DatesAsDoubles = F,
        Filter = "",
        OdbcConnection = "",
        OdbcSqlQuery = "")}}

Julie is a technical support person at Mathsoft and was very helpful.

***************************************************************************
Arnold Dekkers [Arnold.Dekkers at rivm.nl]  suggested that I purchase DBMS copy
pointing
out that it was not expensive ($295 for Windows95) and easy to use. This is
a utility allowing
exchange between many different data formats.  There is a free one
month demo so anyone who wants to test it out can do so.
see http://www.conceptual.com/ for details.

****************************************************************************
*******************************
Andy Cooper suggested just concatenating the worksheets by hand and
inserting names as an additional column.

****************************************************************************
*********************************
Longhow Lam posted his solution to the problem to S-news- it is sort of like
Julie Green's , although
he does  suggest a source (p515 of the program manual) for information about
tab names.

****************************************************************************
************************************
G. Stephen Few was very helpful, and volunteered a macro that he had written
in Visual Basic (much like
what I eventually used, I suspect that can read tab names).
****************************************************************************
********************************
James Roger [James at livedata.co.uk] suggested "OLE automation between Excel
(VBA macro code) and S-Plus to push the data from the VBA end" citing
success with SAS in this way. As near as I can tell this is kind of close to
the VB program we wrote here.
****************************************************************************
*****************
Nick Locantore [nick at Waratah.com] was very helpful but experienced the same
kind of problems I had with reading the test
file until I specified   **NameRow = "0"** as a parameter. Why this needs to
be done I don't know.
Hope this solves your problem, Nick. 
****************************************************************************
********
As a postscript, I did try to read the file in "The Splus way" but although
the sample
workbook worked fine, the workbook with 26 sheets is still not working
right-Splus reports that the selected cells
are empty. I don't really have an interest in pursuing this further since I
solved the problem with Visual Basic but would be
interested in hearing from anyone who worked with Splus to import a really
messy workbook.

Thanks to all correspondents.

Fred Balch

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Adjusting strip spacing in trellis plot
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: Adjusting strip spacing in trellis plot
messages.body_plain:
(With apologies: I neglected to indicate a subject in my original post.)

I received one helpful suggestion from Marcel Baumgartner
<marcel.baumgartner at rdls.nestle.com>.  Marcel suggests that I create

   my.strip.default <-  strip.default

and then adjust the value y from 0.5 to 0.6 in

   do.call("text", c(list(x = 0.5, y = 0.5),
      labels =strip.names), par.strip.text)

Note that there is a corresponding do.call("text"...) component in each
'style' of my.strip.default.

Then use my.strip default in the call to the trellis plot:

   strip = function(...) my.strip.default(...,style=1)

This suggestion approximated my desired result by moving the strip text
upwards a bit inside the strip.  Close, but my real goal was to increase
the size of the strip, so I dug a little deeper.  After some poking, I
settled on the following.

In render.trellis, change definition of strip.labels.width to:

  strip.labels.width <-
     sum(par("csi") * (1.4 + is.fac * 0)) * show.strip

The value 1.4 gives a nice bit of "extra" space.  The default value is
1, which leads to the crowding I was concerned about.

(incidentally, could anyone explain why is.fac * 0 is there?)

I believe the safe way to implement this would be to:
1.  make a copy of print.trellis called my.print.trellis
2.  make a copy of render.trellis called my.render.trellis
3.  make the above change in my.render.trellis and change
    my.print.trellis to call my.render.trellis.

Thanks to Marcel for the suggestion which got me started, and if anyone
has any comments, I'd be glad to hear them.  I get nervous when I start
fiddling with functions like render.trellis...

Rob

----- Original message -------

I'm using S-PLUS 2000(r2) in Win98.

When I use xyplot(y ~ x | group.var), the dimensions of the strip are
such that the strip labels are vertically "squished".  Rather like when
the line spacing in a paragraph is too small for the font size.

The gui version of similar graphs is more aesthetically pleasing because
the strip labels have a small amount of white space above and below the
text.

Would anyone have any suggestions about how to recreate this spacing in
xyplot?

Or have I simply missed the directions somewhere in the documentation...

Please respond privately, and I will summarise to the list.

Thanks,

Rob

messages.subject: [S] Point process simulation
messages.body_plain:
I'm simulating a point process using SPLUS 2000 under:
1) Win98 on a 400 MHz w/ 128mb
2) NT4 on a 733 MHz w/ 384mb
3) NT4 on a 733 MHz w/ 128mb

In general, the 733s seem to perform the simulations 2.5 to 3 times faster
than the 400 unless SPLUS starts using virtual memory. In which case Win98
seems to manage memory much better than NT4 resulting in faster simulation
times on the Win98 machine than the 733 w/ 128mb. Have other SPLUS users
encounter this? Does it make sense?

Regarding simulating point processes: Cressie in Statistics for Spatial Data
cites a finding by Prof Ripley that simulating a homogenous poisson process
in 2D using two [0,1) uniform random numbers can yield regular patterns. I
am using this approach and I noticed the make.pattern function in the SPLUS
Spatial module also uses this approach. Is this an issue I should be
concerned with? I'm actually simulating a poisson cluster process
(Neyman-Scott process) which is an option in make.pattern. Does anyone know
what cluster distribution assumptions the make.pattern(process="cluster") is
using. I've looked in various SPLUS books and manuals but can't seem to find
good documentation on make.pattern. I could get away from simulating the
process if I could get a handle on the (in Cressie's terminology) zero
probability functional for a poisson cluster process. Could anyone provide
guidance on references that could help.

Thanks!

Tom Stockton

cheers,
Kevin

ORIGINAL QUESTION

Dear S-news,

Can anyone recommend software for demonstrating Bayesian inference.    I've
toyed with BUGs but wonder if there isnt something more appropriate for
introductory level instruction.  Something user friendly and within the Splus
platform would be ideal, although other platforms permitting one to "look at the

mechanics" (the code) would be fine.

release 1).

posting but could not find it in the archives).

I will be happy to post a summary of the responses

thanks in advance,

Kevin

messages.subject: Re: [S] Date: Fri, 18 Feb 2000 11:41:37 +0100
messages.body_plain:
On Fri, 18 Feb 2000, Piot Michel wrote:

> 
> Hi S-Plus Users,
> 
> can anybody explain to me this strange results:
> 
> > seq(from=-1.4, to=0,by=.2)
> [1] -1.400000e+000 -1.200000e+000 -1.000000e+000 -8.000000e-001
> -6.000000e-001 -4.000000e-001
> [7] -2.000000e-001  2.220446e-016
> 
> > seq(from=-1.6, to=0,by=.2)
> [1] -1.6 -1.4 -1.2 -1.0 -0.8 -0.6 -0.4 -0.2  0.0
> 
> Does anybody know, if the rouding problem with 0 is machine dependent or if
> it is a general problem in S-Plus?

Well, I see you are using Windows, but you should tell us!

The problem is general, and in your expectations rather than the results.
-1.4 cannot be represented exactly as a binary fraction:

> print(-1.4, digits=17)     
[1] -1.3999999999999999
> print(seq(from=-1.4, to=0,by=.2), digits=17)
[1] -1.3999999999999999e+00 -1.2000000000000000e+00 -9.9999999999999989e-01
[4] -7.9999999999999982e-01 -5.9999999999999987e-01 -3.9999999999999991e-01
[7] -1.9999999999999973e-01  2.2204460492503131e-16
> print(seq(from=-1.6, to=0,by=.2), digits=17)
[1] -1.60000000000000009 -1.40000000000000013 -1.20000000000000018
[4] -1.00000000000000000 -0.80000000000000004 -0.60000000000000009
[7] -0.39999999999999991 -0.19999999999999996  0.00000000000000000

on my system.  This is not a `rouding problem'; rather it is normal
in floating-point computations. You would do better with

rev(seq(0, -1.4, by=-0.2))

as using smaller numbers first reduces the effect.

-- 
Brian D. Ripley,                  ripley at stats.ox.ac.uk
Professor of Applied Statistics,  http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~ripley/

Oxford OX1 3TG, UK                Fax:  +44 1865 272595

messages.subject: Re: [S] Date: Fri, 18 Feb 2000 11:41:37 +0100
messages.body_plain:
At 2/18/00 at 05:58 AM, Prof Brian D Ripley wrote:

> On Fri, 18 Feb 2000, Piot Michel wrote:
>
>
>
> > can anybody explain to me this strange results:
> >
> > > seq(from=-1.4, to=0,by=.2)
> > [1] -1.400000e+000 -1.200000e+000 -1.000000e+000 -8.000000e-001
> > -6.000000e-001 -4.000000e-001
> > [7] -2.000000e-001  2.220446e-016
>
> The problem is general, and in your expectations rather than the results.
> -1.4 cannot be represented exactly as a binary fraction:
>
> [...]  This is not a `rouding problem'; rather it is normal in
> floating-point computations.

As Brian Ripley stated, such things routinely occur when expressing base-10 
numbers in base 2.  They occur in S-Plus, in Fortran, in C, and so on: it 
is not a language issue.

This imprecision is the reason that Fortran 9x does not allow the use of 
real numbers in DO loops and that Fortran 9x compilers issue warning 
messages when floating-point quantities are used in equality 
comparisons.  Because of base conversion and other technical issues (e.g., 
whether values are stored in main memory or registers), the outcome of such 
operations is unpredictable.

An short article entitled "The Perils of Floating Point" can be found at

http://www.lahey.com/float.htm

While the examples are written in (simple) Fortran, the article should be 
equally interesting to S-Plus users who seek information on this issue.

--
Michael Prager, Ph.D.                <Mike.Prager at noaa.gov>
NOAA Beaufort Laboratory
Beaufort, North Carolina  28516

has built scripts for Helsel's (1990) robust method of censored data
analysis.

method.

populations from singly truncated and double truncated samples:  Annals of
Mathematical Statistics, vol. 21, p. 557-569.

are singly censored or truncated:  Technometrics vol. 1, p. 217-237.

the detection limit: Environmental Science and Technology vl. 24, p.
1755-1774.
Persson, T. and Rootzen, H., 1977, Simple and highly efficient estimators
for a type I censored normal sample:  Biometrika v. 64, p. 123-128.

messages.subject: [S] panel.superpose 5.1 vs. 3.4
messages.body_plain:
While testing Splus 5.1 under Solaris I discovered a difference in
panel.superpose between
Splus 3.4 and v5r1.  The difference occurred while using xyplot with a
grouping and conditioning 
variable in which not all levels of the conditioning variable occur in each
panel.  The following simple 
example illustrates the change:  

  > jj
       w    y     x     z    
       1     1     1     a
       1     2     2     a
       1     3     3     b
       1     4     4     a
       1     5     5     b
       2     6     6     b
       2     7     7     c
       2     8     8     c
       2     9     9     b
       2    10   10     c

 > xyplot(y ~ x | w,  groups=z,  data=jj,  panel=panel.superpose)

Using Splus 3.4 the colors of the points in the first panel corresponding to
z=a and z=b 
are col=2 and col=3, respectively.  In the second panel the colors of the
points
corresponding to z=b and z=c are col=3 and col=4.  The colors are consistent
with
respect to the levels of z across the panels.  Using 5.1, on the other hand,
the colors
in the first panel are the same as those using 3.4, but in the second panel
the colors of 
the points corresponding to z=b and z=c are col=2 and col=3, respectively.
Splus 5.1 chooses the 
panel plotting colors and apparently also type, lty, lwd, pch, cex, and font
based on the number of 
levels  of the grouping variable that appear in the panel rather than the
total number of levels
of the grouping factor.
    I'm tempted to just create my own version of panel.superpose, but before
I do I'd like to 
understand why the change to panel.superpose was made.  I have been unable
to reach anyone
at Mathsoft so I thought I'd try here.

Thanks for the help,

Bill Glynn
glynn_bill at emc.com

messages.subject: [S] Re: seq and floating point (was: a meaningless subject line)
messages.subject_clean: [S] Re: seq and floating point (was: a meaningless subject line)
messages.body_plain:
Michel Piot wrote:

>can anybody explain to me this strange results:
>
>> seq(from=-1.4, to=0,by=.2)
>[1] -1.400000e+000 -1.200000e+000 -1.000000e+000 -8.000000e-001
>-6.000000e-001 -4.000000e-001
>[7] -2.000000e-001  2.220446e-016
>
>> seq(from=-1.6, to=0,by=.2)
>[1] -1.6 -1.4 -1.2 -1.0 -0.8 -0.6 -0.4 -0.2  0.0
>
>Does anybody know, if the rouding problem with 0 is machine dependent or if
>it is a general problem in S-Plus?

As Brian Ripley and Michael Prager pointed out, this occurs because
of floating point arithmetic.

Note that 
        seq(from=a, to=b, by=c)
is not guaranteed to have the last value approximately equal to `b'.
In some cases this is desirable, e.g. I often use:
        seq(from=.5, to=n, by=1)/n
to get numbers equally-spaced between 0 and 1:
> seq(.5, 10)/10
 [1] 0.05 0.15 0.25 0.35 0.45 0.55 0.65 0.75 0.85 0.95
In other cases it is not desirable.

If you want the last value of result to be exactly equal to `b',
use
        seq(from=a, to=b, length=round((b-a)/by))

Tim Hesterberg

messages.subject: [S] Power, SS -- STPLAN (It's free)
messages.body_plain:
STPLAN

STPLAN performs power, sample size, and related calculations needed to
plan  studies.   Parameters of   a  test  include those  necessary  to
describe the distributions  under the null and alternative hypotheses,
sample sizes, significance  levels, and power.   Given values for  all
but one   parameter,  STPLAN will  calculate  the  value of  that  one
parameter.  STPLAN provides calculations for 25 hypothesis tests.

A new version (mainly bug fixes) is expected within a few weeks.

messages.subject: [S] Summary for "GLM coefficient estimates"
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-news,

Many thanks to the following experts for their reposnses in regard of
the GLM coefficient estimates.
Your helps solved my problem, to which it might otherwise take me ages
to find a right answer. I
really appreciate your help and thank you all again.

Bill Venables
Nick Ellis
Greg Snow
John Fox
NicoleDepriest
Don Mckenzie
Liaw Andy

As some colleagues emailed me and expressed their interests in the
answers to my question, I
reprinted below the origianl question and responses.

ORIGINAL QUESTION:
============================================
Hi everyone,
I have great difficulties with the explanation of the coefficient
estimates of a GLM. To my knowledge, I understand that the coefficients
represent the means of the factor in a series. For example, I have a
factor "Year" that has a time of ten years. The GLM would produce ten
estimates: Intercept, year1, year2,...year9. The Intercept is the mean
of first year, "year1" is the mean of Year 2 relative to Year 1, and its

abosolute mean should be "Intercept+year1", and so on. Am I right?

However, the example S-Plus gave in its manual (S-Plus 4 Guide to
Statistics page 213) can not be explained this wage. A GLM with the data

of "solder.balance", the "Opening" factor has three levels, S, M, L. The

coefficients estimated are: Intercept=0.438,
Opening.L=-1.687,Opening.Q=0.462. The confusion here is what Opening.Q
means. If in order, Intercept shoudl refer to Opening at S level because

S is the first level in the data file, and then Opening.Q should mean
Opening at M level. If this is right, the mean of M level shoudl be the
highest and that of L level should be the lowest. But, the graph S-Plus
produced for the Openging effect was: S highest, M mediate, and L
lowest, which is consistent with the data file.

Your can easily test this with the command:
>paov2 <-glm(skips~.+(Opening+Solder+Mask+PadType)^2,
family=poison,data=solder.balance)
>summary(paov2)
>par(mfrow=c92,3)
>plot.gam(paov2,resid=T)

Can anybody expalin how the coefficient estimates and the graph should
be explained?

Thank you very much for your help.

RESPONSES:
===============================================
>>From Bill Venables <William.Venables at cmis.CSIRO.AU

Dear Yimin,

You have sent me at least one message about this problem directly
but I have been away from my email for some time now and unable
to reply.

No.  If you want coefficient estimates that correspond to this
interpretation you should begin your S-PLUS session with

> options(contrasts = c("contr.treatment", "contr.poly"))

This ensures that the model matrices will be constructed the way
you want them to be, otherwise you get different (but equivalent)
model matrices and the coefficients are relative to that.

When you fit a model, if you have any doubts about the
coefficients you should always look at the model matrix using

> model.matrix(obj)

where obj is the fitted model object, and make certain you can
explain the model matrix that you see.  It is very easy to
mistake what sort of model matrix is being used (as you have).

There is another complication with ordered factors, too.  That is
where the "contr.poly" comes in.  I suspect you have some reading
and study ahead of you.

Note that plot.gam does not plot coefficients.  It plots the
additive contributions to the linear predictor from the term
involved.  This is always independent of the contrasts used. This
is also something for you to sort out, and it may take some time,
unfortunately.  There is a lot to cover before you sort this kind
of issue out fully.

--
Bill Venables,      Statistician,     CMIS Environmetrics Project
CSIRO Marine Labs, PO Box 120, Cleveland, Qld,  AUSTRALIA.   4163

========================
Greg Snow <snow at statsci.com

The coefficients computed depend on which contrasts are being used.  The

default contrasts are helmert contrasts for unordered factors (each
treatment level is compared to the mean of all previous levels) and
polynomial contrasts for ordered factors.

What you describe above is treatment contrasts (these are not the
default
but can be specified in different ways).

Opening is coded as an ordered factor so the default is to use
polynomial
contrasts.  Opening.L is the linear contrast and Opening.Q is the
quadradic contrast.

you should probably look up more information on contrasts (or always use

treatment contrasts
options(contrasts=c("contr.treatment","contr.treatment"))

======================
>>From Nicole Depriest <ntd at stat.ohio-state.edu

What you need to submit prior to running glm is
     options(contrasts=c("contr.treatment","contr.poly"))
Then you should be able to interpret the estimates the way you would
like.

Nicole DePriest

==============================
John Fox  < jfox at McMaster.ca

Dear Yimin Ye,

S constructs contrasts (columns of the model matrix) for a factor
according to the contrasts option.
The default option is

> options()$contrasts
          factor      ordered
 "contr.helmert" "contr.poly"

that is Helmert contrasts for an unordered factor, and orthogonal
polynomials for an ordered factor.

Opening is a three-category ordered factor (with therefore 2 df), and
Opening.L and Opening.Q
are, respectively, the linear and quadratic terms. Try
contrasts(Opening) to see the contrast coding,
here:

> contrasts(Opening)
          .L         .Q
S -0.7071068  0.4082483
M  0.0000000 -0.8164966
L  0.7071068  0.4082483

By the way, Helmert contrasts do not simply treat the first category as
the baseline -- to do this you
need to use "treatment" contrasts, contr.treatment. You can change the
global option, or assign a
contrast attribute to the factor:

> contrasts(Opening)<-contr.helmert(3)
> contrasts(Opening)
  [,1] [,2]
S   -1   -1
M    1   -1
L    0    2
>
> contrasts(Opening)<-contr.treatment(3)
> contrasts(Opening)
  2 3
S 0 0
M 1 0
L 0 1

See ?contrasts and ?contr.treatment for more information.

plot.gam shows partial residuals and partial effect plots. These don't
depend on the coding of
contrasts.

I hope that this helps,

John
=============================
Nick Ellis <nick.ellis at marine.csiro.au
Bill Venables has posted an excellent tutorial on contrasts, which I
attach
below.

Nick Ellis

-----Original Message-----
From: Bill Venables [mailto:wvenable at attunga.stats.adelaide.edu.au]
Sent: Saturday, 29 March 1997 16:54
To: Wei Qian
Cc: S-news at utstat.toronto.edu
Subject: Re: test contrasts [long]

Wei Qian writes:

 > I am new to Splus, so please don't be offended if my question is
 > too naive.

We're all friends here, Wei.  It's not that kind of group...mostly.

 > Does anyone know how to test contrasts in Splus?  To be specific,
 > suppose I have a one-way layout experiment with 3 treatments, and
 > I want to test the contrasts of treatment 1 vs. treatment 2,
 > treatment 1 vs. treatment 3, etc.  In SAS, I could use the
 > following:
 >
 > proc glm;
 >     class trt;
 >     model y = trt;
 >     contrasts "1 vs. 2" 1 -1 0;
 >     contrasts "2 vs. 3" 1 0 -1;
 > run;
 >
 > One way I can think of is that to construct my design matrix and
 > obtain the contrast sum of squares through a series of matrix
 > operations, but is there any easy way to do it or any built-in
 > function in Splus can do it?

The answer is `yes' but hardly anyone seems to know how to do it.
The explanation in the `white book' for example, seems a little
incomplete to me and not quite adequate to settle the case you
raise.  (The explanation in the yellow book is also inadequate,
but I hope come July we will have fixed that.)  Since this is one
of the most frequent questions people ask me in direct email,
too, let me try (again) to sort it out in some detail.

A formula such as y ~ f, where f is a factor in principle
generates a single classification model in the form

        y_{ij} = mu + phi_i + e_{ij}

Write the design matrix in the form X = [1 Xf], where, assuming f
has p levels, Xf is the n x p dummy variable (ie binary) matrix
corresponding to the phi_i's.  So in matrix terms the model is
written as

        y = 1 mu  +  Xf phi  +  e

(a) If you remove the intercept term, using y ~ f - 1, then Xf is
    the design matrix you get and the coefficients correspond to
    the class means.

(b) If the intercept term is left in, then the design matrix X
    does not have full column rank, so an adjustment has to be
    made to Xf to make it so.

The redundancy comes about because the columns of Xf add to the
the 1-vector, that is Xf 1_p = 1_n.  So let C be any p x (p - 1)
matrix such that [1 C] is nonsingular.  It can easily be seen
that Xc = [1 (Xf C)] will have full column rank and that fitting
the model using this model matrix is equivalent to the original
redundantly specified model.  The matrix C is called the *coding
matrix* for the factor f.

The linear model is actually fitted in the form

        y = 1 mu + (Xf C) alpha + e

where alpha has (p-1) components, of course.  In order to make
sense of the alpha's we need to relate them back to the phi's.

For any such C there will be a vector, v, such the v'C = 0'
(using ' for transpose).  (In fact v spans the orthogonal
complement to the column space of C).  Clearly phi and alpha are
related by

        C alpha  =  phi

but since v'C = 0', it follows that an identification constraint
applies, namely v'phi = 0.  By multiplying both sides by
(C'C)^{-1} C', it also follows that

        alpha = (C'C)^{-1} C'phi

which provides an interpretation for the alpha's in terms of the
(constrained) phi's.

For example take the Helmert contrasts.

> contr.helmert(4)
  [,1] [,2] [,3]
1   -1   -1   -1
2    1   -1   -1
3    0    2   -1
4    0    0    3

The constraint vector is clearly v = (1,1,1,1), since the columns
add to zero.  In this case the columns are also mutually
orthogonal, so the matrix (C'C)^{-1) C' (the generalized inverse
of C) has a similar form apart from a few row divisors:

> fractions(ginverse(contr.helmert(4)))
      [,1]  [,2]  [,3]  [,4]
[1,]  -1/2   1/2     0     0
[2,]  -1/6  -1/6   1/3     0
[3,] -1/12 -1/12 -1/12   1/4

(ginverse() will be available in S+4.0 and fractions(), now
available in the MASS2 library, simply displays numbers in
fractional form so that patterns are more obvious).

Thus the phi's are identified by requiring that they add to zero,
and

        alpha_1 = (phi_2 - phi_1)/2,
        alpha_2 = [phi_3 - (phi_1 + phi_2)/2] / 3

&c.  When the columns of C are not mutually orthogonal the story
is not quite so obvious, though.  For example take a C matrix
using contr.sdif (available in the MASS2 library)

> contr.sdif(4)
  [2-1] [3-2] [4-3]
1 -0.75  -0.5 -0.25
2  0.25  -0.5 -0.25
3  0.25   0.5 -0.25
4  0.25   0.5  0.75

The column sums are all zero so the identification constraint is
still the same, but they are not mutually orthogonal.  The
coefficients do have an easy interpretation, though:

> fractions(ginverse(contr.sdif(4)))
     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,] -1    1    0    0
[2,]  0   -1    1    0
[3,]  0    0   -1    1

Thus alpha_i = phi_(i+1) - phi_i, the "successive differences" of
phi's, or equally of class means.

Now (at last) returning to your case.  In specifying the
contrasts you want to have as the coefficients, you are
specifying not C, but (C'C)^{-1} C' (say M).  So what you need to
do is work backwards, noting that C is also the ginverse of M:

> M <- rbind(c(1,-1,0), c(1, 0, -1))
> M
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1   -1    0
[2,]    1    0   -1
> fractions(ginverse(M))
     [,1] [,2]
[1,]  1/3  1/3
[2,] -2/3  1/3
[3,]  1/3 -2/3

This is the C matrix you need to specify as the coding matrix.
Note that (of course) the columns add to zero so that the implied
constraint on the phi's is that they sum to zero.

Since ginverse() is not yet published code, here is a quick and
dirty version that is adequate for this kind of case (but don't
push it...)

ginv <- function(M)
        if(nrow(M) < ncol(M)) t(ginv(t(M)))
        else solve(crossprod(M), t(M))

So all you need to do is as follows:

> M <- rbind(c(1, -1, 0), c(1, 0, -1))
> Cmat <- ginv(M)
> dimnames(Cmat) <- list(NULL, c("1 vs 2", "1 vs 3")) # optional
> contrasts(trt) <- Cmat
> fm <- aov(y ~ trt,  .....)

The easy way to see the single degrees of freedom components is:

> summary.lm(fm)$coef

and the partitioned anova table can be shown using:

> summary(fm, split = list(trt = list("1 vs 2" = 1, "1 vs 3"= 2)))

Finally you can see the complete phi-style representation of the
fitted model by

> dummy.coef(fm)

(Unfortunately dummy.coef does not generate an effective variance
matrix for the coefficients, otherwise contrasts could be directly
tested after the fitting process.  This could be fixed, though.)

Note that the standard contrast functions contr.helmert,
contr.poly and contr.sum (as well as out contr.sdif) all impose
the same identification constraint on the phi's, i.e. they add to
1, but contr.treatment is different as it corresponds to phi_1 =
0.  So the phi parameters mean different things in this case, but
the same principle applies.  If the rows of M all add to zero
(making them `conventional contrasts') so will the columns of C =
M'(MM')^{-1}, (obviously).

Bill Venables.

Thanks.  Don

Since glm's inherit from lm's, the dummy.coef method for lm's should

automatically) for glm's -- at least I think that this is correct.

for
 a categorical factor does not correspond to the actual levels of that

and

messages.subject: [S] Summary for "GLM coefficient estimates"
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-news,

Many thanks to the following experts for their reposnses in regard of
the GLM coefficient estimates.
Your helps solved my problem, to which it might otherwise take me ages
to find a right answer. I
really appreciate your help and thank you all again.

Bill Venables
Nick Ellis
Greg Snow
John Fox
NicoleDepriest
Don Mckenzie
Liaw Andy

As some colleagues emailed me and expressed their interests in the
answers to my question, I
reprinted below the origianl question and responses.

ORIGINAL QUESTION:
============================================
Hi everyone,
I have great difficulties with the explanation of the coefficient
estimates of a GLM. To my knowledge, I understand that the coefficients
represent the means of the factor in a series. For example, I have a
factor "Year" that has a time of ten years. The GLM would produce ten
estimates: Intercept, year1, year2,...year9. The Intercept is the mean
of first year, "year1" is the mean of Year 2 relative to Year 1, and its

abosolute mean should be "Intercept+year1", and so on. Am I right?

However, the example S-Plus gave in its manual (S-Plus 4 Guide to
Statistics page 213) can not be explained this wage. A GLM with the data

of "solder.balance", the "Opening" factor has three levels, S, M, L. The

coefficients estimated are: Intercept=0.438,
Opening.L=-1.687,Opening.Q=0.462. The confusion here is what Opening.Q
means. If in order, Intercept shoudl refer to Opening at S level because

S is the first level in the data file, and then Opening.Q should mean
Opening at M level. If this is right, the mean of M level shoudl be the
highest and that of L level should be the lowest. But, the graph S-Plus
produced for the Openging effect was: S highest, M mediate, and L
lowest, which is consistent with the data file.

Your can easily test this with the command:
>paov2 <-glm(skips~.+(Opening+Solder+Mask+PadType)^2,
family=poison,data=solder.balance)
>summary(paov2)
>par(mfrow=c92,3)
>plot.gam(paov2,resid=T)

Can anybody expalin how the coefficient estimates and the graph should
be explained?

Thank you very much for your help.

RESPONSES:
===============================================
>>From Bill Venables <William.Venables at cmis.CSIRO.AU

Dear Yimin,

You have sent me at least one message about this problem directly
but I have been away from my email for some time now and unable
to reply.

No.  If you want coefficient estimates that correspond to this
interpretation you should begin your S-PLUS session with

> options(contrasts = c("contr.treatment", "contr.poly"))

This ensures that the model matrices will be constructed the way
you want them to be, otherwise you get different (but equivalent)
model matrices and the coefficients are relative to that.

When you fit a model, if you have any doubts about the
coefficients you should always look at the model matrix using

> model.matrix(obj)

where obj is the fitted model object, and make certain you can
explain the model matrix that you see.  It is very easy to
mistake what sort of model matrix is being used (as you have).

There is another complication with ordered factors, too.  That is
where the "contr.poly" comes in.  I suspect you have some reading
and study ahead of you.

Note that plot.gam does not plot coefficients.  It plots the
additive contributions to the linear predictor from the term
involved.  This is always independent of the contrasts used. This
is also something for you to sort out, and it may take some time,
unfortunately.  There is a lot to cover before you sort this kind
of issue out fully.

--
Bill Venables,      Statistician,     CMIS Environmetrics Project
CSIRO Marine Labs, PO Box 120, Cleveland, Qld,  AUSTRALIA.   4163

========================
Greg Snow <snow at statsci.com

The coefficients computed depend on which contrasts are being used.  The

default contrasts are helmert contrasts for unordered factors (each
treatment level is compared to the mean of all previous levels) and
polynomial contrasts for ordered factors.

What you describe above is treatment contrasts (these are not the
default
but can be specified in different ways).

Opening is coded as an ordered factor so the default is to use
polynomial
contrasts.  Opening.L is the linear contrast and Opening.Q is the
quadradic contrast.

you should probably look up more information on contrasts (or always use

treatment contrasts
options(contrasts=c("contr.treatment","contr.treatment"))

======================
>>From Nicole Depriest <ntd at stat.ohio-state.edu

What you need to submit prior to running glm is
     options(contrasts=c("contr.treatment","contr.poly"))
Then you should be able to interpret the estimates the way you would
like.

Nicole DePriest

==============================
John Fox  < jfox at McMaster.ca

Dear Yimin Ye,

S constructs contrasts (columns of the model matrix) for a factor
according to the contrasts option.
The default option is

> options()$contrasts
          factor      ordered
 "contr.helmert" "contr.poly"

that is Helmert contrasts for an unordered factor, and orthogonal
polynomials for an ordered factor.

Opening is a three-category ordered factor (with therefore 2 df), and
Opening.L and Opening.Q
are, respectively, the linear and quadratic terms. Try
contrasts(Opening) to see the contrast coding,
here:

> contrasts(Opening)
          .L         .Q
S -0.7071068  0.4082483
M  0.0000000 -0.8164966
L  0.7071068  0.4082483

By the way, Helmert contrasts do not simply treat the first category as
the baseline -- to do this you
need to use "treatment" contrasts, contr.treatment. You can change the
global option, or assign a
contrast attribute to the factor:

> contrasts(Opening)<-contr.helmert(3)
> contrasts(Opening)
  [,1] [,2]
S   -1   -1
M    1   -1
L    0    2
>
> contrasts(Opening)<-contr.treatment(3)
> contrasts(Opening)
  2 3
S 0 0
M 1 0
L 0 1

See ?contrasts and ?contr.treatment for more information.

plot.gam shows partial residuals and partial effect plots. These don't
depend on the coding of
contrasts.

I hope that this helps,

John
=============================
Nick Ellis <nick.ellis at marine.csiro.au
Bill Venables has posted an excellent tutorial on contrasts, which I
attach
below.

Nick Ellis

-----Original Message-----
From: Bill Venables [mailto:wvenable at attunga.stats.adelaide.edu.au]
Sent: Saturday, 29 March 1997 16:54
To: Wei Qian
Cc: S-news at utstat.toronto.edu
Subject: Re: test contrasts [long]

Wei Qian writes:

 > I am new to Splus, so please don't be offended if my question is
 > too naive.

We're all friends here, Wei.  It's not that kind of group...mostly.

 > Does anyone know how to test contrasts in Splus?  To be specific,
 > suppose I have a one-way layout experiment with 3 treatments, and
 > I want to test the contrasts of treatment 1 vs. treatment 2,
 > treatment 1 vs. treatment 3, etc.  In SAS, I could use the
 > following:
 >
 > proc glm;
 >     class trt;
 >     model y = trt;
 >     contrasts "1 vs. 2" 1 -1 0;
 >     contrasts "2 vs. 3" 1 0 -1;
 > run;
 >
 > One way I can think of is that to construct my design matrix and
 > obtain the contrast sum of squares through a series of matrix
 > operations, but is there any easy way to do it or any built-in
 > function in Splus can do it?

The answer is `yes' but hardly anyone seems to know how to do it.
The explanation in the `white book' for example, seems a little
incomplete to me and not quite adequate to settle the case you
raise.  (The explanation in the yellow book is also inadequate,
but I hope come July we will have fixed that.)  Since this is one
of the most frequent questions people ask me in direct email,
too, let me try (again) to sort it out in some detail.

A formula such as y ~ f, where f is a factor in principle
generates a single classification model in the form

        y_{ij} = mu + phi_i + e_{ij}

Write the design matrix in the form X = [1 Xf], where, assuming f
has p levels, Xf is the n x p dummy variable (ie binary) matrix
corresponding to the phi_i's.  So in matrix terms the model is
written as

        y = 1 mu  +  Xf phi  +  e

(a) If you remove the intercept term, using y ~ f - 1, then Xf is
    the design matrix you get and the coefficients correspond to
    the class means.

(b) If the intercept term is left in, then the design matrix X
    does not have full column rank, so an adjustment has to be
    made to Xf to make it so.

The redundancy comes about because the columns of Xf add to the
the 1-vector, that is Xf 1_p = 1_n.  So let C be any p x (p - 1)
matrix such that [1 C] is nonsingular.  It can easily be seen
that Xc = [1 (Xf C)] will have full column rank and that fitting
the model using this model matrix is equivalent to the original
redundantly specified model.  The matrix C is called the *coding
matrix* for the factor f.

The linear model is actually fitted in the form

        y = 1 mu + (Xf C) alpha + e

where alpha has (p-1) components, of course.  In order to make
sense of the alpha's we need to relate them back to the phi's.

For any such C there will be a vector, v, such the v'C = 0'
(using ' for transpose).  (In fact v spans the orthogonal
complement to the column space of C).  Clearly phi and alpha are
related by

        C alpha  =  phi

but since v'C = 0', it follows that an identification constraint
applies, namely v'phi = 0.  By multiplying both sides by
(C'C)^{-1} C', it also follows that

        alpha = (C'C)^{-1} C'phi

which provides an interpretation for the alpha's in terms of the
(constrained) phi's.

For example take the Helmert contrasts.

> contr.helmert(4)
  [,1] [,2] [,3]
1   -1   -1   -1
2    1   -1   -1
3    0    2   -1
4    0    0    3

The constraint vector is clearly v = (1,1,1,1), since the columns
add to zero.  In this case the columns are also mutually
orthogonal, so the matrix (C'C)^{-1) C' (the generalized inverse
of C) has a similar form apart from a few row divisors:

> fractions(ginverse(contr.helmert(4)))
      [,1]  [,2]  [,3]  [,4]
[1,]  -1/2   1/2     0     0
[2,]  -1/6  -1/6   1/3     0
[3,] -1/12 -1/12 -1/12   1/4

(ginverse() will be available in S+4.0 and fractions(), now
available in the MASS2 library, simply displays numbers in
fractional form so that patterns are more obvious).

Thus the phi's are identified by requiring that they add to zero,
and

        alpha_1 = (phi_2 - phi_1)/2,
        alpha_2 = [phi_3 - (phi_1 + phi_2)/2] / 3

&c.  When the columns of C are not mutually orthogonal the story
is not quite so obvious, though.  For example take a C matrix
using contr.sdif (available in the MASS2 library)

> contr.sdif(4)
  [2-1] [3-2] [4-3]
1 -0.75  -0.5 -0.25
2  0.25  -0.5 -0.25
3  0.25   0.5 -0.25
4  0.25   0.5  0.75

The column sums are all zero so the identification constraint is
still the same, but they are not mutually orthogonal.  The
coefficients do have an easy interpretation, though:

> fractions(ginverse(contr.sdif(4)))
     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,] -1    1    0    0
[2,]  0   -1    1    0
[3,]  0    0   -1    1

Thus alpha_i = phi_(i+1) - phi_i, the "successive differences" of
phi's, or equally of class means.

Now (at last) returning to your case.  In specifying the
contrasts you want to have as the coefficients, you are
specifying not C, but (C'C)^{-1} C' (say M).  So what you need to
do is work backwards, noting that C is also the ginverse of M:

> M <- rbind(c(1,-1,0), c(1, 0, -1))
> M
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1   -1    0
[2,]    1    0   -1
> fractions(ginverse(M))
     [,1] [,2]
[1,]  1/3  1/3
[2,] -2/3  1/3
[3,]  1/3 -2/3

This is the C matrix you need to specify as the coding matrix.
Note that (of course) the columns add to zero so that the implied
constraint on the phi's is that they sum to zero.

Since ginverse() is not yet published code, here is a quick and
dirty version that is adequate for this kind of case (but don't
push it...)

ginv <- function(M)
        if(nrow(M) < ncol(M)) t(ginv(t(M)))
        else solve(crossprod(M), t(M))

So all you need to do is as follows:

> M <- rbind(c(1, -1, 0), c(1, 0, -1))
> Cmat <- ginv(M)
> dimnames(Cmat) <- list(NULL, c("1 vs 2", "1 vs 3")) # optional
> contrasts(trt) <- Cmat
> fm <- aov(y ~ trt,  .....)

The easy way to see the single degrees of freedom components is:

> summary.lm(fm)$coef

and the partitioned anova table can be shown using:

> summary(fm, split = list(trt = list("1 vs 2" = 1, "1 vs 3"= 2)))

Finally you can see the complete phi-style representation of the
fitted model by

> dummy.coef(fm)

(Unfortunately dummy.coef does not generate an effective variance
matrix for the coefficients, otherwise contrasts could be directly
tested after the fitting process.  This could be fixed, though.)

Note that the standard contrast functions contr.helmert,
contr.poly and contr.sum (as well as out contr.sdif) all impose
the same identification constraint on the phi's, i.e. they add to
1, but contr.treatment is different as it corresponds to phi_1 =
0.  So the phi parameters mean different things in this case, but
the same principle applies.  If the rows of M all add to zero
(making them `conventional contrasts') so will the columns of C =
M'(MM')^{-1}, (obviously).

Bill Venables.

Thanks.  Don

Since glm's inherit from lm's, the dummy.coef method for lm's should
work (and be invoked
automatically) for glm's -- at least I think that this is correct.

John
==========================

for
 a categorical factor does not correspond to the actual levels of that

 coefficient corresponds to the difference between the means of year1
and

year3
 and the average of year1 and year2, and so on.  For details, see the
Guide
 to Statistics, Vol.1, Ch. 16, page 553.  The discussion is for linear

messages.subject: Re: [S] Generalized GAM
messages.body_plain:
Dear Pierre,

The model 

Z = s1(X) + s2(X)*Y + error

can be fitted with using loess() if you don't mind the dependence between
the smoothers.  The method is what Cleveland on page 341 in "Chambers &
Hastie (1991): Statistical Models in S, Wadsworth:CA" call a conditionally
parametric surface.  The call to loess() will look something like:

S> loess(Z ~ X*Y, degree=2, parametric="Y", drop.square="Y")

This will result in a local quadractic approximation of the function
corresponding to s1 and a local linear approximation corresponding to
s2.  If you want a local linear approximation for s1 I think adding
drop.square="X" should work.  

-----
The rest of this e-mail does not qualify for "a direct way":

When there is more explanatory variables using loess() gets difficult
and it is not possible to approximate eg. s2 with a local quadractic
since the degree argument must be 0, 1, or 2.  However, the same
approach to estimation could be applied.  If you need this you can
download LFLM from my page http://www.imm.dtu.dk/~han/software.html,

don't share arguments then "Hastie & Tibshirani
(1993). Varying-coefficient Models. JRSS-B, Vol. 55, No. 4,
pp. 757-796" has the answer.  I don't know software which can do this,
but for specific models and not too big data sets you have the
building blocks (smoothers) already in S-PLUS.

messages.subject: [S] Summary: transporting Excel w missing
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Stephen Few, Mike Chotkowski, and Chuck Berry for their
replies.  The most complete answer comes from Chuck Berry:  

...

The old fashioned way to do this is to 'save as ...' the EXCEL file, then
scan() or read.table() from Splus. Usually, leaving the cells of the EXCEL
worksheet unfilled will work if you 'save as *.csv' (providing that commas
aren't used in data elements in any cell - if so, I think you can choose
another delimiter from the 'save as' dialog or one of the properties
menus). 

One headache is that EXCEL sometimes get a little smarter than you
really want it to be: If you have a spreadsheet in which the last k cells
of a row are not filled in, then EXCEL just forgets about those k cells,
inserts a newline, and happily moves on. This leaves you with 'ragged'
rows that read.table will choke on. My admittedly low-tech solution to
this is to add a dummy column to such a spreadsheet with a dummy element
('EOL', say) in each cell. This forces the row to be completed with enough
commas to maintain a rectangular format. Also, I recall that having the
last element in a row of data be null (so the record ends with ",\n")
causes a hiccup for read.table that the dummy column avoids.

I have occasionally had to use the 'EOL' string to reconstruct records
when someone sent me files that had newlines arbitrarily inserted in some
records. I can't remember exactly how this came about - EXCEL or JMP *.csv
files were emailed as attachments, possibly after being 'binhex'ed as
Mac's are wont to do. Anyway, using Perl one can define any arbitrary
string as the 'end-of-line-on-input' or some such, do a string replace of
newline with null, then output the result defining 'end-of-line-on-output'
or whatever as the unix newline, Ctrl-j.

Instead of all this, if you do decide to fill empty cells with a string,
just about anything will do provided that it doesn't duplicate something
that is legitimate data. You can specify na.strings=... in read.table. I
recall that this can be a vector, so multiple values are allowed.

Hope this helps.

Regards,

Chuck Berry

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I apologise in advance if the solution to the following 
problem is obvious, but I'd appreciate any suggestions.

Suppose I have a set of n observations, and I want to 
find out all possible unique ways in which I can split 
these observations into r groups of equal size n/r.
 
For example if I have n=4 observations {1, 2, 3, 4} and I 
split these into r=2 groups I can have

{1, 2} {3, 4}

messages.subject: Re: [S] Generalized GAM
messages.body_plain:
Pierre Joyet wrote:
>Is there (in S-Plus 4.5) a direct way of fitting a model such as
>
>Z = s1(X) + Y * s2(X)
>
>where X and Y are continuous variables, * is the usual multiplication, and
>s1 and s2 are smooth functions to be determined? Can gam be brought to do
>that or must a specific backfitting procedure be written?

Trevor Hastie provided a wonderful solution to problems like this --
to use regression splines, e.g. bs() or ns() (rather than s() or lo()).  E.g.
        lm(Z ~ bs(X) + Y * bs(X))
You can specify the degrees of freedom or the knots.  You could also do e.g.
        glm(Z ~ s(X) + Y * bs(X))

Trevor also suggested "Varying Coefficient Models", if you don't want
to use regression splines, but that is harder to implement.

Trevor Hastie wrote on 24 Nov 93:
>In response to Tim Hesterberg's two model enquiries:
>
>> (2) I would like to fit a model with a scaled smooth
>>         y = s(x1,x2) * x3 + (other additive terms) + residuals
>> where s() is a smooth function of two variables and the "*" 
>> indicates standard multiplication rather than S formula
>> notation. 
> 
>You may wish to see the Hastie and Tibshirani paper in JRSSB 1993 on
> "Varying Coefficient Models", for ideas on model (2). 
>Our algorithm is essentially that given by Tim -- note that when the 
>denominator is near zero, so are the weights.
>We don't have standard software installed for these models ala S modelling 
>functions, but in principle this is possible.
>I had it on my pile of things to do but then the pile fell over ....
>
>One simple approach in messy situations like this is to abandon loess or
>smoothing splines and use natural regression splines. In Tim's case he
>wants a function of two variables, calling for tensor products:
>
>glm( y ~ ns(x1,df=5):ns(x2,df=5):x3  + other terms, family = robust)
>for example, might do. I encluded the "robust" family in case thats 
>what was wanted, otherwise lm() could do as well. It would be up to 
>the user  to sort out the coefficients etc, bit I've done this before
> and its not too hard. 
>
>> (1) I would like to fit a model of the form
>>         y = F(x2) - F(x1) + residuals
>> where F() is a smooth function, and the same function is used for
>> both x1 and x2.  x1 and x2 are very highly correlated.
>
>I looked at a problem like problem (1) in the past, and had an idea on how
> to fit it. For example, one can pose the appropriate smoothing spline version
>of the problem and come up with a natural expression for the solution.
>
>But again, natural splines come to the fore with a simple approach:
>
>fit1 <- glm( y ~ I(ns(x1, knots) + ns(x2, knots)), family = robust)
>and then your fitted function is cbind(1,ns(.,knots))%*% coef(fit1)

messages.subject: Re: [S] xyplot command - summary
messages.body_plain:
I would like to thank Lutz Prechelt and  Bill Venables for their  response
to my question
about plotting (x,y) locations and  a boundary using the  xyplot command.
There appears to be two ways of doing this:

1) Perhaps the simplest one would be

xyplot(xboundary ~ yboundary, xlab = "x", ylab = "y",
      panel = function(x, y, ...) {
            panel.xyplot(x, y, ..., type = "l")
            panel.xyplot(xlocations, ylocations, pch=1, col=2, ...)
      })
- Prechelt and  Bill Venables

This assumes that your x's and y's are free-standing vectors on
the search path.

2)  A second  solution is to put xlocations and xboundary together in the
same data frame,
and similarly for y, and have a factor, say `type' that distinguishes them.
You could then do

xyplot(x ~ y, dat, panel = function(x, y, ...) {
 panel.xyplot(x[dat$type == "b"], y[dat$type == "b"], ..., type = "l")
 panel.xyplot(x[dat$type == "l"], y[dat$type == "l"], ..., pch=1, col=2)
})

That looks much more complicated than the first way, but it pays
off if you want to do a conditioning plot and you need to pass
subscripts down to the panel function.
- Bill Venables.

Many thanks to both.

--

messages.subject: Re: [S] xyplot command - summary
messages.body_plain:
I didn't see the original post but from what I can gather you might also look at
the xYplot in the Hmisc library, which will do error bars, error bands, 
automatic
grouping of x into quantiles with plotting of 3 quantiles of y for each x 
group, etc.
For "error bars" on more than one group of points there is an option to 
alternately
show only the lower or upper error bar for alternating groups.

For example you can say

xYplot(Cbind(y, ylow, yhigh) ~ x | z, groups=g, method='bands')
Key()   # automatic legend for g

Note that Cbind is a special "put multiple variables together for trellis" 
function.
xYplot makes sure that the proper subsets of ylow and yhigh are used for levels
of  z and g.

-Frank

messages.subject: Re: [S] exp
messages.body_plain:
A summary of some responses to my query about exp() producing NA's for
large-valued arguments:

--Original posting--

I wanted to clarify things a bit regarding my last posting (supplied
below).

Patrick Connolly noted that the limit for exp() in 3.4 is

exp(709:710)
[1] 8.218407e+307           Inf

The same limits apply for 5.1.  However, instead of Inf being supplied
(the preferable response) NA's are generated.

> exp(709:710)
[1] 8.218407e+307            NA
Warning messages:
  NAs generated in: exp(x)

I was just wondering if anyone had encountered this problem before and if
it has a workaround.  Otherwise, I'll wait for the next release :)

--Replies--

(1)
Siem Heisterkamp noted that

In S-plus 2000 on w95 the  response is:
 exp(709:710)
[1] 8.218407e+307           Inf
as was in your message for 3.4

which implies it may be a 5.1 issue.  

(2)
On Tue, 22 Feb 2000, Michael Prager wrote:

...
> At the risk of stating the obvious, could you not write your own function 
> that returns exp(x) when x<=709 and Inf otherwise?  That would seem to be a 
> reasonable workaround (though I agree it should be unnecessary).
> 
> Regards,
> ...Mike Prager
> 

(3)
On Tue, 22 Feb 2000, Rolf Turner wrote:

...
> Suggested workaround: Mask/over-write exp() with
>
>       exp <- function(x) {
>               ifelse(x <= 709,.Internal(exp(x),"do_math",T,108),Inf)
>       }
>
> There's a possibility that you'll ***still* see NAs for values of x > 709;
> this would indicate that the problem is with print() --- Infs are being
> ***printed*** as NAs.  I have vague recollections of this happening to
> me in some other context.

I did try masking and it does work.

> exp2(1000)
[1] Inf
Warning messages:
  NAs generated in: exp(x)

Thanks for all the help,

Nicole

messages.subject: [S] multivariate regression routines ??
messages.body_plain:
I need a hardy, fast regression solver for GENERAL multivariate linear
regression setups. (By "GENERAL", I mean to include all of the linear
regession cases mentioned in Box and Tsiao, 1973, viz. cases with a
(possibly) different design matrix for each regressand, some common
regression coefficients (shared by two or more regressands), and some
regression coefficients that pertain to only one regressand.)

I prefer for this to be a routine that can be called from S+/R or for
C/Fortran code components that can be readily adapted for this
purpose. And if it computes marginal HPD regions for the regression
parameters and other useful summaries, that would be still better.

If I fail to find such a routine, I will probably adapt a general
purpose non-linear solver or IRLS solver. Advice would be appreciated
(beyond that in the later chapters of Box and Tsiao, 1973). In
particular, if anyone knows (a reference to) useful decomposition
techniques that capitalize on special structure, I'd like to know. (I
am thinking here that since the 'common design matrix' case has simple
structure, there may be a useful approach that breaks the computation
into a piece that has a common design matrix with no common parameters
and a piece that does not, solves each piece in turn conditioning on
the other, etc. But any advice is welcome.)

Chuck Berry

messages.subject: Re: [S] Data frame subsetting question
messages.body_plain:
Debbie Carlson <dcarlson at neptuneandco.com> writes:

> I'm using S-PLUS 2000 on Windows '98 machine, but I've also run into this 
> on Unix Solaris machines.
> 
> I've managed in about 8 years of programming in Splus to ignore this, but,
> alas, no longer.  When creating a new data frame that is a subset of an
> existing one, I don't want all of the attributes of the old data frame,
> just the ones that apply to the new data frame.
> How can I achieve this?

Well that makes two of us who tried to avoid that problem for a long
time.  I didn't know how to do this properly until I read a draft
version of the new book "S Programming" by Venables and Ripley (to be
published in April 2000 - see
              http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/MASS3/Sprog/
or the North American mirror
            http://franz.stat.wisc.edu/pub/MASS3/Sprog/).

> Example code follows for a data frame in which one of the variables is
> ANALYTE and there are 225 ANALYTES possible.
> 
> > dim(Sedgrer2)
> [1] 37200 26
> 
> > ind_Sedgrer2$ANALYTE=="ZINC" &
> Sedgrer2$AREA!="SF Bay Reference Location" & Sedgrer2$METHOD!="CLP
> INORGANICS-ROUT-SEMETAL" 
> 
> > dat_Sedgrer2[ind,]
> >unique(dat$ANALYTE)
> [1] ZINC
> Levels (first 5 out of 225):
> [1] "0.075 MM" "0.106 MM" "0.250 MM" "0.425 MM" "0.850 MM"

Replace

 dat$ANALYTE <- dat$ANALYTE[, drop = TRUE]

When subsetting a factor or an ordered factor the optional argument
drop = TRUE means to reduce the levels in the factor from the original
set to only those levels that occur in the subset.

messages.body_plain:
Nicole swears to a final posting. But not I!
Nicole expresses a preference for Inf to be returned.
Tim Hesterberg expresses a preference for NA.

(I wonder how it is that Inf should be considered "incorrect" and 
also how Inf might propagate through subsequent computations. And how 
it is that Inf is less correct than NA. I would think that Inf might 
be more Informational [grin] than NA. But these are digressions. My 
real question is:)

Is there not an IEEE standard for floating point calculations that 
specifies what should be returned? (If I were at work I'd try to look 
it up, but I'm at home at present.)

Like it or not, if there is a standards document with some degree of 
agreed-upon international authority, that is what I would go with.

-Don

messages.subject: [S] Question on weighted non-linear regression
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-plus Users,

I received three suggestions. Thanks to Marcel, Don MacKenzie and Peter ellis.

The solutions :

nls( ~sqrt(W) * (f(x)-x)), where W are the weights, and f(x) the nonlinear
function you want to fit.

Note:there is no weight argument in nls(). See Venables and Ripley for
a workaround (page 270 2nd edition)

Another suggestion is also stated below. 

Thanks.

Abd Rahman Kassim
Hill Forest Silviculture
Forest Research Institute Malaysia (FRIM)
Kepong 52109 
Kuala Lumpur

==========
I presume you want to fit a non-linear model because
you believe the response "bag" is normally distributed
before being put through the log transform.  You can
have the effect of a non-linear model in this instance
by fitting a GLM (generalized linear model) with a
gaussian distribution and a log link, which I think is
equivalent to your nls model.  S+ glm function does
not allow you to do this directly (only identity link
allowed with gaussian family), but the same effect can
be achieved by using a quasi-likelihood distribution
with variance = constant (ie the same mean to variance
relationship as a gaussian model).  The code would be:

fit.glm <- glm(bag ~ bat + log(bat) + idp1 +
idp2,family=quasi(variance=constant, link=log),
weights=bat^w)

Of course, this is just a convenient work-around
because your model can be easily linearised.

My question was:
============

How can I write S-code for weighted nls using the
example shown below. I'm using the parameter estimates
from the linear regression for the nls function.

fit <- lm(log(bag) ~ bat + log(bat) + idp1 +
idp2,weights=bat^w)
b0 <- as.numeric(fit$coeff[1])
b1 <- as.numeric(fit$coeff[2])
b2 <- as.numeric(fit$coeff[3])
b3 <- as.numeric(fit$coeff[4])
b4 <- as.numeric(fit$coeff[5])

nls.st <- c(b0 , b1 , b2 , b3 , b4)

nls.fm <- nls(bag ~ exp(b0) * (exp(b1 * bat)) * (bat^
b2) * exp(b3 * idp1) * exp(b4 * idp2), start = ls.st,
trace = T)

messages.subject: Re: [S] Missing factor levels and predict.
messages.body_plain:
One approach would be to make a prediction that is un-conditioned on that
variable, as you have no way to make an estimate for a cell that didn't
exist in the training data.  With the Design library contrast function it is 
easy
to get predictions like this, with confidence intervals:

# In a model containing age, race, and sex,
# compute an estimate of the mean response for a
# 50 year old male, averaged over the races using
# observed frequencies for the races as weights

f <- ols(y ~ age + race + sex)
contrast(f, list(age=50, sex='male', race=levels(race)),
         type='average', weights=table(race))

It would not be too hard do this with predict() for any S-Plus method,
if you also get the "predicted" design matrix so that you can average its rows
to compute the proper variances of weight or unweighted marginal predicted
means.  The marginal means are estimated expected values in the absence
of knowledge of the factor in question.  -Frank

messages.body_plain:
Timothy R. Johnson writes:

> 
> Hello all.
> 
> I am confused about how deriv() works in comparison to deriv3() (from
> the V&R MASS library). I'm using S-PLUS version 4.5, release 2, for MS
> Windows.

deriv3() may be in the MASS library now, but it is there by kind
permission of the author, David M. Smith, now of MathSoft UK.

> I want to use deriv() to return a function that will give me the
> gradient of a specified function. I try deriv(),
> 
> > foo1 <- deriv(z ~ 2*x + 3*y, c("x","y"), function(x,y) {})
> > foo1
> function(x, y)
> {
>  .value <- (2 * x) + (3 * y)
>  .actualArgs <- match.call()[c("x", "y")]
>  if(all(unlist(lapply(as.list(.actualArgs), is.name)))) {
>   .grad <- array(0, c(length(.value), 2), list(NULL, c("x", "y")))
>   .grad[, "x"] <- 2
>   .grad[, "y"] <- 3
>   dimnames(.grad) <- list(NULL, .actualArgs)
>   attr(.value, "gradient") <- .grad
>  }
>  .value
> }
> > foo1(1,1)
> [1] 5
> > attr(foo1(1,1), "gradient")
> NULL

It is a bug that was introduced into S-PLUS 4.x and has remained
safely ensconced there ever since, even S-PLUS 5.1 for Unix is
affected.  It seems to be a classic case of fixing something that
simply isn't broken.

Inspection of the code that you now get shows that you can work
around it by using only "name" arguments (not "named" arguments):

> x <- 1; y <- 1
> attr(foo1(x, y), "gradient")
     x y
[1,] 2 3

but you certainly should not have to pussy-foot around it like
that!  More seriously if you put the names the other way round
you get the labels in the output switched:

> attr(foo1(y, x), "gradient")
     y x
[1,] 2 3

which to my mind confuses variables with their values.

deriv3() continues to work because it merely extends the old,
unbroken version of deriv().  We failed to introduce the bug in
question for some reason.  Perhaps we were just too slow....

--

Well, let's see. That's a data matrix (assuming continuous covariates) of
960Mb.  And you will almost certainly need more than one copy, and S has a
design limit of 2Gb of objects (at least on a 32-bit machine, and 64-bit
machines are not currently supported, I think). So I guess no one has
*succeeded*, using lm.

There are other ways, though, to load in the data in blocks and build
up an answer.  But seriously, you don't need anything like that much data
to build up an idea of the patterns on 80 covariates.  Start with a 1%
sample, say.

> And some aggregation of the responses could reduce their number by
> factors of 16 or 100.
